description: We are two first-year college students from the University of Washington. We both enjoy building interesting and unique ideas. If you are interested in building something special or are a creative mind, feel free to join!
summary: We developed a tool to protect property and people from dangerous mudslides. We used the NISAR data to identify burn areas, slopes, and houses through smoke and ash. This is important and impactful because it saves lives and property from mudslides, a hazard that is often overlooked.
details:
When a fire happens, people often focus on the burned area itself, however, the issues that emerge from this fire go beyond just that. Burned trees and foliage on slopes create debris, and the roots that held the soil are gone. When the next heavy rain arrives, mud, rock and burned wood can pour downhill onto the homes below, sometimes months after the fire is out.

Mudwatch is a map that shows which homes sit in the way. It stacks three layers: where the fire burned, where the ground is steep, and where people live. Where all three line up, the map turns red. The burn scar comes from radar satellites, which see through smoke and cloud, so the map works while an ordinary satellite camera still sees only smoke.

We tested it on two 2026 fires. On the East Evans Creek Fire in Oregon, radar confirmed the burn scar eight days after the fire started, and Mudwatch found 17 homes, about 43 people, in a possible mud path. It flagged the first of those homes on July 18, 116 days before the date on the USGS expert assessment, and the two agree on 119 of 150 basins. On the Bradeen Hill Fire in Washington, it found 11 homes, about 28 people.

The site asks whether you are a resident or a first responder. Residents can search their street, see whether their home is at risk, and see which road leads out. First responders also see the points where a mud channel crosses a public road, so crews can clear them before the rain.

The burn scar is mapped from NASA OPERA RTC-S1 radar data and checked against NISAR. Slope comes from NASADEM, and homes and people come from the 2020 Census and USA Structures. The data pipeline is written in Python, and the website is a static page built with MapLibre.

Every number on the site is computed from public data, and the site shows how its results compare with the USGS assessment.
dataRefs: NASA OPERA RTC-S1 (radiometric terrain-corrected Sentinel-1 backscatter), via ASF DAAC
NISAR L2 GCOV L-band backscatter (NASA-ISRO), via ASF DAAC
NASADEM 1 arc-second elevation (NASADEM_HGT v001), LP DAAC
Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) true-colour imagery, via NASA Worldview Snapshots
NASA OPERA DIST-ALERT-S1 (surface disturbance alerts; archive checked, does not yet cover these fires)
NASA Earthdata Login and the earthaccess Python library (data search and download)
projectRefs: Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar (ESA), the source imagery behind OPERA RTC-S1
USGS post-wildfire debris-flow hazard assessments (perimeters, basins, stream segments)
U.S. Census Bureau 2020 Census blocks, population and housing units (TIGERweb)
USA Structures building inventory (FEMA and Oak Ridge National Laboratory)
OpenStreetMap roads, place names and address search (Overpass API, Nominatim), ODbL
MapLibre GL JS web map library
Open-source Python libraries: GeoPandas, Rasterio, SciPy, h5py, Pillow
